subject: math
title: Grade 8 Interest and Credit: Simple and Compound Interest, Credit Cards and Budgets
seo_title: Grade 8 Simple and Compound Interest Worksheets: Credit Cards and Budgets (Free, Answer Key, Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Determine the growth of simple and compound interest at various rates using digital tools, and explain the impact interest has on long-term financial planning
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on interest and credit for the Ontario curriculum: simple interest with I = Prt, compound interest year by year in a table, simple vs compound growth over time, credit card interest, fees and rewards, and budgets and money choices. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Simple interest is found on the principal only; compound interest is found on the new balance each year.
key_sub: Write the rate as a decimal (4% = 0.04). $1000 at 5% compound grows to $1050, then $1102.50, because the interest earns interest. On a credit card, interest is charged only on the part you do not pay by the due date.
body_html:
Simple interest: I = Prt

Interest is money paid for using money. A bank pays you interest on savings. You pay interest when you borrow. Simple interest is found on the principal only, so it is the same every year.

I = Prt: P is the principal, r is the yearly rate as a decimal (3% = 0.03), and t is the time in years (6 months = 0.5 years).

Example

You save $500 at 3% simple interest per year for 2 years. What is the balance?

I = $500 × 0.03 × 2 = $30. Balance: $500 + $30 = $530.

Answer: $530

Compound interest: build a table

With compound interest, each year’s interest is added to the balance. Next year’s interest is found on the new, bigger balance, so you earn interest on interest. Make a table one year at a time (a spreadsheet can do this for you).

Example

$1000 is saved at 5% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?

Year 1: $1000 × 0.05 = $50, so $1050. Year 2: $1050 × 0.05 = $52.50, so $1102.50. In one step: $1000 × 1.05 × 1.05 = $1102.50.

Answer: $1102.50

Simple vs compound over time

Simple interest grows in a straight line. Compound interest curves upward, and the gap gets wider every year. For long-term savings, start early and leave the interest in. For debt, the same growth works against you.

Credit cards

A credit card is borrowed money. Pay the full balance by the due date and no interest is charged on new purchases. Leave part unpaid and interest is charged on it every month (often about 20% a year, close to 2% a month). Paying only the minimum keeps the debt growing. Watch for yearly fees, and check whether rewards really cover them.

Example

A bill is $650 and you pay $150. The card charges 2% interest per month on the unpaid balance. How much interest is added?

Unpaid: $650 − $150 = $500. Interest: $500 × 0.02 = $10.

Answer: $10

Budgets and financial plans

A budget lists money in and money out. Fixed expenses stay the same each month; variable expenses change. Pay yourself first: put savings aside before you spend. Compare choices by their total cost, including interest and fees.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Using the rate as a whole number ($600 × 4)Change the percent to a decimal: 4% = 0.04
Finding compound interest on the original amount every yearFind each year’s interest on the new balance
Giving the interest when the question asks for the balanceBalance = principal + interest
Using months as years (6 months as t = 6)Divide by 12: 6 months = 0.5 years
Finding card interest on the whole billInterest is charged only on the unpaid part

faq.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
faq.a: Simple interest is found on the starting amount only, so it is the same every year. Compound interest is found on the new balance each year, so the interest also earns interest and the money grows faster.

faq.q: How do Grade 8 students calculate compound interest without a formula?
faq.a: They build a table one year at a time: find the interest on the balance, add it, and use the new balance for the next year. A spreadsheet can fill in many years quickly, for example with =B2*1.05 at 5%.

faq.q: What do Grade 8 students learn in financial literacy in Ontario?
faq.a: Grade 8 students compare methods of payment, build financial plans and budgets, find the growth of simple and compound interest, and learn how credit card interest, fees and rewards work.

faq.q: How is interest charged on a credit card?
faq.a: If the full balance is paid by the due date, new purchases have no interest. Any unpaid balance is charged interest, often about 20% a year, and the interest compounds each month until it is paid off.

items.q: What is interest?
c: A tax added to a purchase
Money paid for using someone else’s money
A fee for opening an account
The money you first put in
items.e: Interest is money paid for the use of money. A bank pays you interest on savings, and you pay interest when you borrow.

items.q: In the simple interest formula I = Prt, what does P stand for?
items.e: I is the interest, P is the principal (the amount saved or borrowed), r is the yearly rate as a decimal, and t is the time in years.

items.q: To use I = Prt, how do you write a rate of 4% per year?
items.e: Percent means “out of 100”. 4% = 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04. Using 4 makes the interest 100 times too big.

items.q: How do you write a rate of 2.5% per year as a decimal?
What is the simple interest on $500 at 4% per year for 1 year?
items.e: I = Prt = $500 × 0.04 × 1 = $20. ($2000 uses 4 instead of 0.04; $520 is the balance, not the interest.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $800 at 3% per year for 2 years?
items.e: I = Prt = $800 × 0.03 × 2 = $48. ($24 is only 1 year of interest.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $1200 at 2.5% per year for 3 years?
Nathan saves $600 in an account that pays 5% simple interest per year. What is the balance after 4 years?
items.e: I = Prt = $600 × 0.05 × 4 = $120. Balance: $600 + $120 = $720. ($120 is only the interest; $630 is the balance after 1 year.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $2000 at 1.5% per year for 2 years?
items.e: I = Prt = $2000 × 0.015 × 2 = $60. ($30 is only 1 year of interest.)

items.q: $1000 is saved at 3% simple interest per year. How much interest is earned in the 5th year alone?
items.e: Simple interest is always found on the original $1000, so every year earns the same: $1000 × 0.03 = $30. ($150 is the total for all 5 years; $33.77 would be compound interest.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $900 at 4% per year for 6 months?
items.e: I = Prt = $900 × 0.04 × 0.5 = $18. The time must be in years: 6 months = 6/12 = 0.5 years. ($216 uses 6 as the time; $36 is a full year; $1800 uses 4 instead of 0.04.)

items.q: What is the simple interest on $1000 at 2% per year for 18 months?
items.e: 18 months = 18/12 = 1.5 years. I = $1000 × 0.02 × 1.5 = $30. ($360 uses 18 as the number of years; $20 is only 1 year.)

items.q: $400 earns $14 of simple interest in 1 year. What is the yearly interest rate?
items.e: r = I ÷ (Pt) = $14 ÷ $400 = 0.035. As a percent: 0.035 × 100 = 3.5%. (0.035% forgets to change the decimal back to a percent.)

items.q: $750 earns 4% simple interest per year. How many years until it has earned $90 of interest?
items.e: Interest each year: $750 × 0.04 = $30. $90 ÷ $30 = 3 years. (22.5 comes from $90 ÷ 4; 30 is the dollars of interest per year, not the time.)

items.q: How much must be saved at 3% simple interest per year to earn $60 of interest in 2 years?
items.e: I = Prt, so P = I ÷ (rt) = $60 ÷ (0.03 × 2) = $60 ÷ 0.06 = $1000. Check: $1000 × 0.03 × 2 = $60. ($2000 forgets the 2 years; $3.60 multiplies instead of dividing.)

items.q: Which earns more simple interest: $500 at 3% per year for 4 years, or $800 at 2% per year for 2 years?
items.e: $500 × 0.03 × 4 = $60. $800 × 0.02 × 2 = $32. $500 at 3% for 4 years earns more, even though the principal is smaller: the rate and the time matter too.

items.q: Ava’s family borrows $6000 for a new furnace at 7% simple interest per year. They pay it all back after 3 years. How much do they pay back in total?
A GIC pays 5% simple interest per year on $3600. If the yearly interest is shared equally over 12 months, how much interest is that each month?
items.e: Yearly interest: $3600 × 0.05 = $180. Each month: $180 ÷ 12 = $15. ($180 is the interest for the whole year; $300 is $3600 ÷ 12; $1800 uses 0.5 instead of 0.05.)

items.q: $1000 is saved at 5% simple interest per year. After how many years has the interest earned reached $1000?
items.e: Each year earns $1000 × 0.05 = $50. $1000 ÷ $50 = 20 years. (2 years uses 0.5 instead of 0.05; 200 years comes from $1000 ÷ 5.)

items.q: $500 at 4% simple interest per year for 3 years earns $60. Which of these earns $120?
items.e: Doubling the time doubles simple interest: $500 × 0.04 × 6 = $120. Doubling both the rate and the time makes it 4 times as much ($240). $1000 at 2% for 3 years earns $60, and $500 at 6% for 3 years earns $90.

items.q: What is compound interest?
c: Interest earned on the principal and on earlier interest
Interest paid only at the very end
A rate that goes up every year
Interest that is the same every year
items.e: With compound interest, each year’s interest is added to the balance, and the next year’s interest is found on the new, bigger balance. You earn interest on your interest.

items.q: $1000 is saved at 5% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 1 year?
items.e: Interest for year 1: $1000 × 0.05 = $50. Balance: $1000 + $50 = $1050. ($1500 uses 0.5 instead of 0.05.)

items.q: $1000 is saved at 5% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?
items.e: Year 1: $1000 + $50 = $1050. Year 2: interest on $1050 is $1050 × 0.05 = $52.50, so the balance is $1050 + $52.50 = $1102.50. ($1100 finds the interest on the original $1000 again.)

items.q: The table shows $2000 saved at 4% compound interest per year. What is the interest in year 2?
items.e: Year 2 starts with $2080. Interest: $2080 × 0.04 = $83.20. ($80 uses the original $2000; $8.32 uses 0.004 instead of 0.04.)

items.q: The table shows $3000 at 5% compound interest per year. What goes in the missing cell?
items.e: Each year starts with the balance at the end of the year before. Year 3 starts with $3307.50, the end of year 2. ($3000 restarts from the original amount; $3300 is what simple interest would give.)

items.q: $1000 is saved at 10% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 3 years?
At 3% compound interest per year, each year’s balance is the year before multiplied by what number?
items.e: The new balance is 100% of the old balance plus 3% more: 103% = 1.03. Multiplying by 0.03 gives only the interest; 1.3 would be 30%.

items.q: Which calculation gives the balance after 2 years for $500 at 6% compound interest per year?
items.e: Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.06, so two years is 500 × 1.06 × 1.06 = 561.80. 500 + 500 × 0.06 × 2 = 560 is simple interest; 500 × 1.06 × 2 doubles the money.

items.q: $5000 is saved at 2% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?
Olivia puts $2500 in a savings account at 4% compound interest per year. How much interest does she earn in year 2?
items.e: Year 1: $2500 × 0.04 = $100, so the balance is $2600. Year 2: $2600 × 0.04 = $104. ($100 is year 1 again; $2704 is the balance, not the interest.)

items.q: $800 is saved at 5% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 3 years?
$4000 is saved at 3% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?
The table shows $5000 at 2% compound interest per year. How much interest is earned in all over the 3 years?
items.e: Total interest = final balance − principal = $5306.04 − $5000 = $306.04. (Or add the interest column: $100 + $102 + $104.04.) $300 is what simple interest would give.

items.q: Jayden made a compound interest table for $1000 at 5%. He wrote $50 of interest in every row. What mistake did he make?
c: Starting each year with the new balance
Finding interest on the original $1000 only
Adding the interest to the balance
items.e: $50 every year is simple interest. With compound interest each year’s interest is found on the new balance, so year 2 earns $1050 × 0.05 = $52.50.

items.q: To find 4% interest on $600, Benjamin writes $600 × 4 = $2400. What should he do instead?
items.e: 4% = 0.04, so the interest is $600 × 0.04 = $24. Using 4 makes the interest 100 times too big, and 0.4 is 40%. So multiply by 0.04.

items.q: In a spreadsheet, cell B2 holds the balance at the end of year 1. Which formula gives the balance at the end of year 2 at 5% compound interest per year?
items.e: Multiplying by 1.05 keeps the balance and adds 5% of it. =B2*1.05 can be filled down to make the next years. (=B2*0.05 gives only the interest.)

items.q: The table shows $1000 at 10% compound interest per year. What is the balance at the end of year 4?
items.e: Year 4 interest: $1331 × 0.10 = $133.10. End of year 4: $1331 + $133.10 = $1464.10. ($1400 is simple interest; $1441 adds only $110.)

items.q: $1000 earns 5% compound interest per year: $50 in year 1 and $52.50 in year 2. Why is the interest bigger in year 2?
c: The year 1 interest earns interest too
The rate goes up in year 2
items.e: The rate stays 5%, but year 2 starts with $1050, not $1000. The extra $2.50 is 5% of the $50 earned in year 1: the interest earns interest.

items.q: A family saves $10 000 at 3% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?
Zoe puts $1500 from a summer job into a 3-year GIC that pays 4% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 3 years, to the nearest cent?

sets.title: Simple vs compound interest over time

items.q: The graph shows $1000 growing at 8% per year for 20 years, once with simple interest and once with compound interest. Which line shows compound interest?
items.e: Simple interest adds the same $80 every year, so it makes a straight line. Compound interest adds more each year, so its graph curves upward. The curved line is compound interest.

items.q: Which statement about the graph is true?
c: The lines are the same after 20 years
The gap between the lines grows each year
items.e: Both start at $1000. Each year compound interest earns a little more than the year before, so the gap gets wider and wider. After 20 years compound is about $4661 and simple is $2600.

items.q: $1000 is saved for 2 years at 5% per year. How much more is the balance with compound interest than with simple interest?
items.e: Simple: $1000 + $50 + $50 = $1100. Compound: $1050 + $52.50 = $1102.50. Difference: $2.50, which is the 5% interest on year 1’s $50.

items.q: $2000 is saved for 3 years at 10% per year. How much more is the balance with compound interest than with simple interest?
$800 is saved at 4% per year. After exactly 1 year, how does compound interest compare with simple interest?
items.e: In year 1 both find 4% of the same $800, so both give $832. They are the same after 1 year; compound pulls ahead from year 2 on.

items.q: A spreadsheet shows $1000 growing at 6% per year (balances to the nearest dollar). After 20 years, how much more is the compound balance than the simple balance?
items.e: Compound: $3207. Simple: $2200. Difference: $3207 − $2200 = $1007.

items.q: Use the spreadsheet. How much does the gap between the compound and simple balances grow from year 10 to year 20?
items.e: Year 10: $1791 − $1600 = $191. Year 20: $3207 − $2200 = $1007. The gap is more than 5 times as big: it grows from $191 to $1007. Over a long time, compound interest pulls far ahead.

items.q: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: 72 ÷ the rate. About how many years does it take to double at 6% per year?
items.e: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. Check: $1000 × 1.06 twelve times is about $2012. (66 subtracts 72 − 6; 432 multiplies.)

items.q: $1000 is saved at 6% per year. Which doubles the money first?
c: Both double at the same time
items.e: Simple interest adds $60 a year, so it needs about 17 years to add $1000. Compound interest doubles the money in about 12 years. Compound interest doubles it first.

items.q: Account A pays 4% simple interest per year. Account B pays 3.5% compound interest per year. Which account gives more on $5000 after 2 years?

Account A pays 4% simple interest per year. Account B pays 3.5% compound interest per year. A spreadsheet shows that after 20 years $5000 grows to $9000 in A and about $9949 in B. What does this show?
c: Over a long time, compound can beat a higher simple rate
The two accounts are the same
A higher rate always gives more
items.e: Over 2 years Account A is ahead, but over 20 years Account B is about $949 ahead. For long-term savings, compounding can matter more than a slightly higher simple rate.

items.q: A $500 debt grows at 20% compound interest per year, and no payments are made. How much is owed after 2 years?
items.e: Year 1: $500 + $100 = $600. Year 2: $600 + $120 = $720. ($700 is simple interest.) Compound interest makes unpaid debt grow quickly.

items.q: Why is compound interest good for savers but bad for borrowers?
c: It only applies to savings accounts
Banks never charge it on loans
It makes the rate lower over time
It grows any balance faster, saved or owed
items.e: Compound interest grows the balance faster, whether it is money you have saved or money you owe. That helps savers and hurts borrowers who leave debt unpaid.

items.q: Which choice grows $1000 the most in 10 years?
items.e: From a spreadsheet: 5% simple gives $1500, 4% compound about $1480, 3% compound about $1344, and 5% compound about $1629, the most.

items.q: Arjun says: “$1000 at 5% compound interest for 3 years is $1000 + 3 × $50 = $1150.” What mistake did he make?
c: Finding interest on the original amount only
Adding the interest to the principal
items.e: He used simple interest. With compound interest the balance is $1050, $1102.50, then $1157.63 (to the nearest cent). He found interest on the original amount only.

items.q: Emma saves $2500 for 2 years at 4% per year. How much more does she earn with compound interest than with simple interest?
items.e: Simple: 2 × $100 = $200 of interest. Compound: $100 + $104 = $204 of interest. Difference: $4.

items.q: A spreadsheet shows $1000 with compound interest at 3% and at 6% per year (to the nearest dollar). After 30 years, how much more is in the 6% account?
items.e: $5743 − $2427 = $3316. The rate is only doubled, but the interest earned ($4743 compared with $1427) is more than 3 times as much.

items.q: Lucas puts $1000 into savings at 5% compound interest per year at age 15. Priya puts in $1000 at the same rate at age 25. Both leave it until age 65. Who has more?
items.e: Lucas’s money grows for 50 years; Priya’s grows for 40. A spreadsheet gives about $11 468 and about $7040. Lucas has far more: starting early gives compound interest more time.

items.q: $1000 is saved at 6% compound interest per year. A spreadsheet shows a balance of $3025.60 at the start of year 20. How much interest is earned in year 20, to the nearest cent?
items.e: $3025.60 × 0.06 = $181.536 → $181.54. That is about 3 times the $60 earned in year 1, at the same rate. ($60 uses the original $1000; $3207.14 is the balance, not the interest.)

items.q: Which choice is the best long-term financial plan for saving?
c: Wait to start until you earn more
Start early and leave the interest in
Take the interest out each year
items.e: Compound interest needs the interest to stay in the account and needs time. Starting early and leaving the interest in lets the interest earn interest for many years.

sets.title: Credit cards: interest, fees and rewards

items.q: You pay the full credit card balance by the due date. How much interest do you pay on the new purchases?
items.e: Credit cards in Canada give a grace period of at least 21 days for new purchases. If you pay the full balance by the due date, no interest is charged.

items.q: What happens when you pay only the minimum payment on a credit card?
c: The rest of the bill is cancelled
Interest is charged on the unpaid part
The card company pays the rest
items.e: The minimum payment only keeps the account in good standing. Interest is charged on everything you do not pay, so the debt can last a long time.

items.q: A credit card charges 24% interest per year. About what rate is that per month?
items.e: There are 12 months in a year: 24% ÷ 12 = 2% per month.

items.q: Chloe leaves $400 unpaid on a credit card that charges 2% interest per month on the unpaid balance. How much interest is added after 1 month?
items.e: $400 × 0.02 = $8. ($800 uses 2 instead of 0.02; $408 is the new balance; $80 uses 0.2.)

items.q: Ethan’s credit card bill is $650. He pays $150 by the due date. The card charges 2% interest per month on the unpaid balance. How much interest is added?
items.e: Unpaid balance: $650 − $150 = $500. Interest: $500 × 0.02 = $10. ($13 finds interest on the whole $650; $3 finds it on the $150 that was paid.)

items.q: The minimum payment is $10 or 3% of the balance, whichever is more. What is the minimum payment on this statement?
items.e: 3% of $320 = $320 × 0.03 = $9.60. That is less than $10, so the minimum payment is $10.

items.q: A card’s minimum payment is $10 or 3% of the balance, whichever is more. What is the minimum payment on a balance of $850?
items.e: 3% of $850 = $850 × 0.03 = $25.50. That is more than $10, so the minimum is $25.50. ($255 uses 0.3; $8.50 is only 1%.)

items.q: A credit card gives 1.5% cash back on purchases. A family spends $2400 on the card in a year. How much cash back do they get?
A card has a $120 yearly fee and gives 1% cash back. How much must be spent in a year for the cash back to equal the fee?
items.e: 1% of the spending must be $120. Spending = $120 ÷ 0.01 = $12 000. Check: 1% of $12 000 = $120. ($1200 uses 0.1 instead of 0.01.)

items.q: A purchase on a US website is charged as $80.00 in Canadian dollars. The card adds a 2.5% foreign transaction fee. How much is the fee?
items.e: $80.00 × 0.025 = $2.00. ($200 uses 2.5 instead of 0.025; $82 is the total with the fee.)

items.q: Card A has no yearly fee and gives 0.5% cash back. Card B has a $99 yearly fee and gives 2% cash back. A family spends $6000 a year on the card. Which card leaves them better off?
items.e: Card A: $6000 × 0.005 = $30. Card B: $6000 × 0.02 = $120, minus the $99 fee = $21. Card A is better by $9. Big rewards do not always beat the fee.

items.q: Hana leaves $500 on a credit card that charges 2% interest per month and makes no payments. Interest is added each month. What is the balance after 2 months?
items.e: Month 1: $500 × 0.02 = $10, so $510. Month 2: $510 × 0.02 = $10.20, so $520.20. Credit card interest compounds: you pay interest on interest. ($520 uses $10 both months.)

items.q: A credit card charges 19.99% interest per year. About how much interest is charged on $1000 left unpaid for a year? (Ignore the monthly compounding.)
items.e: $1000 × 0.1999 = $199.90. That is almost $200 extra, about one fifth of the debt. ($19.99 uses 0.01999.)

items.q: A store credit card charges 1.5% interest per month on the unpaid balance. $800 is left unpaid. How much interest is added in 1 month?
items.e: $800 × 0.015 = $12. ($1200 uses 1.5; $120 uses 0.15; $812 is the new balance, not the interest.)

items.q: Which way of paying takes money straight from your own bank account, so you are not borrowing?
items.e: A debit card uses money already in your bank account. Credit cards and pay-later plans are borrowed money that you must pay back.

items.q: Which card can only spend the money that was loaded onto it ahead of time?
items.e: A prepaid card is loaded with money first, so you cannot spend more than that or owe interest. It lets you shop online without borrowing.

items.q: A store offers a $180 jacket as 4 payments of $45 with no interest, but charges a $10 fee for each late payment. Maya is late with 2 payments. How much does the jacket cost in total?
Which habit helps a person build a good credit history?
c: Paying only some bills on time
Paying the full bill on time every month
Using as much of the limit as possible
items.e: Lenders look at how you have handled credit. Paying the full bill on time every month shows you are reliable and also avoids interest.

items.q: A card gives 1 reward point for every $1 spent, and 100 points are worth $1. How much are the points worth after $1000 of purchases?
items.e: $1000 gives 1000 points. 1000 ÷ 100 = $10. That is the same as 1% back.

items.q: The card charges 2% interest per month on the unpaid part of the previous balance. What is the new balance?
items.e: Unpaid: $450 − $200 = $250. Interest: $250 × 0.02 = $5. New balance: $250 + $5 + $120 = $375. ($370 forgets the interest; $379 finds interest on the whole $450.)

items.q: In a monthly budget, which is a fixed expense?
items.e: A fixed expense is the same amount every month, like a phone plan, rent or a bus pass. The others change from month to month (variable expenses).

items.q: Mateo earns $240 a month babysitting. His plan is to save 20% first. How much does he save each month?
How much of Noah’s money is not planned for yet?
items.e: Money in: $200 + $120 = $320. Money out: $35 + $50 + $60 + $45 + $80 = $270 (savings is planned money too). $320 − $270 = $50. ($130 forgets the savings.)

items.q: Liam wants a $900 laptop. He has $300 saved and saves $75 a month. How many more months until he can buy it?
items.e: Still needed: $900 − $300 = $600. $600 ÷ $75 = 8 months. (12 months forgets the $300 already saved.)

items.q: Aiden wants a $600 bike. Choice 1: save $100 a month and buy it in 6 months. Choice 2: buy it now with a store plan of 12 payments of $55. How much more does Choice 2 cost?
items.e: Choice 2: 12 × $55 = $660. Choice 1: $600. $660 − $600 = $60 more. Buying now costs extra; waiting saves money. ($45 compares the monthly amounts, $100 − $55; $660 is the total, not the extra.)

items.q: A financial plan says a family should keep an emergency fund equal to 3 months of expenses. The family spends $2400 a month. How big should the fund be?
items.e: 3 × $2400 = $7200. ($800 divides by 3 instead of multiplying.)

items.q: What does “pay yourself first” mean in a budget?
c: Spend your pay on the first day
Put money into savings before spending
items.e: When money comes in, move your savings amount first, then plan spending with what is left. Saving becomes a habit instead of whatever is left over.

items.q: Leah saves $50 a month for college for 4 years. Without interest, how much will she have?
items.e: 12 months × 4 years = 48 months. 48 × $50 = $2400. ($200 uses 4 months; $600 is only 1 year.)

items.q: For an RESP, the Canada Education Savings Grant adds 20% of what is put in each year (up to $500 a year). Parents put in $2000 this year. How much is the grant?
items.e: 20% of $2000 = $2000 × 0.2 = $400. That is less than $500, so the full $400 is added. ($2400 is the total with the grant.)

items.q: A family borrows $12 000 for a used car at 5% simple interest per year for 3 years. How much interest do they pay?
items.e: I = $12 000 × 0.05 × 3 = $1800. ($600 is only 1 year; $13 800 is the total paid back.)

items.q: Amira buys a $900 phone on a credit card that charges 20% interest per year and pays nothing for a year. About how much is owed after 1 year? (Ignore the monthly compounding.)
items.e: Interest: $900 × 0.2 = $180. Owed: $900 + $180 = $1080. Saving up first would have cost $180 less.

items.q: A family earns $6000 a month. Rent is $1800 a month. What percent of the income goes to rent?
Owen can play hockey for $450 this season, or ringette for $380 plus $90 for equipment. Which costs less, and by how much?
items.e: Ringette: $380 + $90 = $470. Hockey: $450. $470 − $450 = $20, so hockey costs $20 less. (Ringette by $70 forgets the equipment.)

items.q: Kai’s grandparents put $2000 aside for him at 4% per year for 10 years. A spreadsheet shows $2800 with simple interest and $2960 with compound interest (to the nearest dollar). How much more does compounding give?
items.e: $2960 − $2800 = $160. ($960 is all the compound interest; $800 is all the simple interest.)

items.q: $800 sits in a savings account at 3% simple interest per year for the 3 months of summer. How much interest does it earn?
items.e: 3 months = 3/12 = 0.25 years. I = $800 × 0.03 × 0.25 = $6. ($72 uses 3 as the years; $24 is a full year.)

items.q: Mei saves $15 every week for a year. How much does she save?
items.e: A year has 52 weeks: 52 × $15 = $780. ($180 uses 12, the number of months; $720 uses 48 weeks.)

items.q: Sofia works a summer job at $17 an hour, 20 hours a week, for 8 weeks. She saves 40% of the pay. How much does she save?
Nathan has $1000 in savings earning 2% per year and owes $1000 on a credit card at 20% per year. If he uses the savings to pay off the card, about how much better off is he each year?
items.e: He stops paying $1000 × 0.2 = $200 of interest, but gives up $1000 × 0.02 = $20 of interest earned. $200 − $20 = $180 better off each year. High-interest debt is usually the first thing to pay off.

items.q: Which is a need in a family budget for a Canadian winter?
items.e: A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy. Winter boots that fit keep feet warm and dry; the others are wants.

items.q: Ava’s family saves $3000 for a canoe trip in 2 years in an account that pays 2% compound interest per year. How much will they have?
items.e: Year 1: $3000 × 0.02 = $60, so $3060. Year 2: $3060 × 0.02 = $61.20, so $3121.20. ($3120 finds interest on the original $3000 both years.)
